title: CDC Confirms Third US Measles Death as Cases Pass 4,400 and Pennsylvania Warns on Pregnancy Risks
excerpt: Pennsylvania says five residents have died, not three, and has alerted doctors to congenital measles after 66 pregnant women were infected in the country's largest outbreak.
body:
• The CDC has added a third US measles death to its national tracker for 2026; confirmed cases stood at 4,410 as of October 15 across 47 jurisdictions.
  • Pennsylvania, the centre of the largest outbreak, counts five measles-associated deaths — a public dispute with the CDC over how deaths are defined and reported.
  • Pennsylvania warned doctors on October 19 about congenital measles, identified for the first time in decades, after 66 pregnant women were infected since April.
  • Guidance: MMR vaccine must not be given during pregnancy; nonimmune pregnant women exposed to measles should receive immunoglobulin within six days.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed a third measles death in the United States this year, adding it to the national tracker as total confirmed cases for 2026 passed 4,400, according to Becker's Hospital Review. The Department of Health and Human Services told Reuters the count was updated after the National Center for Health Statistics verified measles as the underlying cause of a death; the CDC database does not say when or where that death occurred.

As of October 15, the CDC had confirmed 4,410 cases, with 42 outbreaks reported this year, 96% of cases associated with outbreaks, and cases in 47 jurisdictions — the largest US measles resurgence in decades for a disease declared eliminated in 2000.

The Pennsylvania dispute: three deaths or five?

The federal number sits below the count in the outbreak's epicentre. Pennsylvania's health department has officially reported five measles-associated deaths, while the CDC dashboard includes only three, noting the number is "subject to change" as the agency works with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a standardised case definition for measles deaths, CNN reported.

The disagreement has been running for weeks. Pennsylvania began formally requesting a CDC Epi-Aid field team in September; Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen wrote that the state would rescind the request if the CDC could not "transparently and accurately communicate information about those measles-associated deaths." In a later letter accepting the Epi-Aid, she again asked the CDC to acknowledge the five deaths "so that we can repair and rebuild trust in the public health system." Public health experts say the fight matters beyond bookkeeping: how deaths are counted shapes how seriously the public treats the outbreak.

A warning doctors have not needed in decades

The newest clinical concern is pregnancy. On October 19 the Pennsylvania Department of Health issued an advisory warning physicians about congenital measles — infection passed from mother to baby in the womb — identified for the first time in decades. The department has recorded 66 measles cases in pregnant women since April; state law prevents it from releasing pregnancy outcomes, so the number of congenital cases has not been disclosed. About one-third of babies born to mothers whose measles rash began within 14 days of delivery develop congenital measles, the advisory said.

The guidance for clinicians and families is specific. The MMR vaccine should not be given during pregnancy, and women should avoid pregnancy for 28 days after vaccination. Nonimmune pregnant women exposed to measles should receive immunoglobulin within six days. Babies born within 14 days of a mother's rash onset should be isolated, tested and given immunoglobulin, and infants of mothers who had measles in pregnancy should be monitored for delayed complications.

What families should do

Measles spreads through the air and can linger in a room for up to two hours after an infected person leaves. Two doses of MMR are about 97% effective — the protection gap in this outbreak is overwhelmingly among the unvaccinated. Anyone unsure of their vaccination status, especially those travelling to or living in outbreak areas or planning a pregnancy, should check records with their doctor now rather than after an exposure, when the six-day immunoglobulin window starts running.
